FFAR Research to Test Fogging Approach to Reduce Avian Influenza Transmission Researchers are testing an innovative, plant-based approach to reduce transmission of avian influenza PUBLISHED ON September 15, 2026 Avian influenza has severe economic consequences for the U.S. poultry and egg industries. The virus spreads rapidly among birds and leads to mass depopulation of infected flocks. (Photo by Andrey Tikhonovskiy on Unsplash) Discover more Health Consult Online Doctors Bird INDIANAPOLIS, Ind. — H5N1 influenza, commonly known as bird flu, continues to threaten U.S. poultry and egg production. The Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research (FFAR) and Entomol Products, LLC are investing $448,940 in a Rapid Outcomes from Agricultural Research (ROAR) grant to test an innovative, plant-based approach to reduce transmission of avian influenza. Researchers are determining whether intermittently fogging or misting hydrogenated catmint oil (HCO), a product with demonstrated antiviral properties, in poultry housing can interrupt transmission of avian influenza viruses. Avian influenza has severe economic consequences for the U.S. poultry and egg industries. The virus spreads rapidly among birds and leads to mass depopulation of infected flocks. This influenza virus is classified as High or Low Pathogenic Avian Influenza based on how it affects poultry. Highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses cause severe disease and high mortality in infected poultry, while low pathogenic avian influenza is a mild or asymptomatic viral infection. “Producers need practical solutions to reduce avian influenza transmission that work with existing infrastructure to protect their flocks and limit losses,” said Dr. Jasmine Bruno, FFAR scientific program director. “As fogging is a widely used practice in poultry houses, we want to know if it’s a promising mechanism for protecting birds.” HCO is a modified plant essential oil and an EPA-registered active ingredient used in commercially available insect repellents. Previous research found that aerosolized formulations containing HCO significantly reduced H1N1 influenza virus in the air. Led by Dr. David Hallahan, chief science officer at Entomol, and Dr. Ekramy Sayedahmed, assistant professor of poultry medicine at Purdue University, researchers are testing whether HCO can reduce avian influenza transmission. The researchers are using low pathogenic avian influenza to evaluate HCO’s antiviral effects against avian influenza and inform its potential application against highly pathogenic avian influenza. The team is also establishing effective aerosol delivery parameters, including HCO concentration, fogging duration and frequency, effective range and overall efficacy. “Entomol’s hydrogenated catmint oil technology has demonstrated the ability to disrupt influenza viruses in the air and on surfaces at very low concentrations, said Dr. Hallahan. “This FFAR-supported project will allow us to rigorously evaluate its potential as a practical biosecurity tool for poultry producers.” Discover more Book Wildlife Safaris Choose Bird Feeders HEALTH FFAR is investing in this research to support the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s research priority on Increasing Profitability of Farmers and Ranchers. This research aims to develop a practical, science-driven intervention that strengthens national readiness for avian influenza outbreaks and protects U.S. poultry producers’ livelihoods. FFAR’s ROAR program rapidly funds research and outreach in response to emerging or unanticipated threats to the U.S. food supply or agricultural systems. Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research The Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research (FFAR) builds public-private partnerships to fund bold research addressing big food and agriculture challenges. FFAR was established in the 2014 Farm Bill to increase public agriculture research investments, fill knowledge gaps and complement the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s research agenda. FFAR’s model matches federal funding from Congress with private funding, delivering a powerful return on taxpayer investment. content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, September 17, 2026 EID Journal: Experimental Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus Infection in Alpacas, 2026 #19,338 In 2024 - just over 2 months after the discovery of HPAI H5N1 in U.S. dairy cattle - the USDA reported that HPAI H5N1 had been Detected In Alpacas from a premises (in Idaho) where HPAI-affected poultry had recently been depopulated. Alpacas belong the the family Camelidae, which includes 3 types of camels ( dromedary camels, Bactrian camels, wild Bactrian camels), and 4 lamoids (llama, alpaca, guanaco, and vicuña). Camelidae - including both camels and alpacas - are known to be susceptible to MERS-CoV (see EID Journal: MERS-CoV Antibodies In Alpacas - Qatar), but less is known about their susceptibility to influenza A viruses. In recent years we've seen the mammalian host range of HPAI continue to expand, with the virus detected in horses, pigs, goats, sheep, mink, dogs, and cats and a growing list of peridomestic animals (see below). Some animals are clearly more susceptible than others to the virus, and some appear to be dead-end hosts; susceptible to infection but unlikely to contribute to the spread of of the virus. In an attempt to determine how vulnerable Alpaca are to the virus, and their ability to carry, and shed the virus, researchers at Germany's FLI (Friedrich-Loeffler-Institut) experimentally infected 6 alpaca with the HPAI H5N1 genotype B3.13 (`bovine') virus. While they found that H5N1 B3.13 can induce a mild, but productive, upper respiratory infection in alpacas (including nasal shedding of the virus for several days and seroconversion), it still isn't established whether alpacas can efficiently transmit virus to one another. That said, there would seem to be enough here to warrant inclusion of camelids in farm biosecurity and surveillance plans. Due to its length, I've only posted the highlights. Follow the link to read the report in its entirety. Research Experimental Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus Infection in Alpacas, 2026 Jacob Schön , Angele Breithaupt, Nico Joel Halwe, Maxi Hertel, Ann Kathrin Ahrens, Andrea Aebischer, Donata Hoffmann, and Martin Beer Abstract Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b virus continues to spread globally and sporadically transmits from avian reservoirs to mammalian hosts. In May 2024, H5N1 infections in young goats and alpacas in the United States were reported. Nevertheless, the overall susceptibility of camelids to clade 2.3.4.4b virus remains unclear. We conducted a controlled experimental infection study in 6 alpacas, assessing clinical signs, viral shedding, tissue distribution, and serologic responses after intranasal inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype B3.13 virus. Observed illness was generally mild; body temperature increased slightly and food intake reduced for up to 3 days postinfection. We detected viral RNA in nasal swab samples and confirmed infectious HPAI H5N1 virus. Immunohistochemistry and RNA in situ hybridization detected virus only in the nasopharyngeal tonsil and nasal conchae at 4 days postinfection. Our findings suggest alpacas are susceptible to productive H5N1 infection, highlighting implications for livestock surveillance and biosecurity in regions with ongoing circulation. (SNIP) We experimentally confirmed that alpacas can be intranasally infected with a bovine HPAIV H5N1 B3.13 isolate, leading to subsequent nasal shedding of infectious virus. IHC and ISH confirmed H5N1 virus replication in the nasopharyngeal tonsil and the nasal conchae. Productive infection was corroborated by seroconversion at 20 dpi. We detected individual variation of neutralizing antibody levels, but the small number of animals does not enable general conclusions. The infection did not cause fever, but alpacas reduced feed intake. Whether the viral load shed by the alpacas would be sufficient to cause transmission to contact animals remains undetermined. Intermittent viral RNA detection and low viral titer at 3 dpi might reflect technical variability of the sampling procedure rather than reduced shedding. Our data did not suggest that alpacas replicate H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b genotype B3.13 virus with exceptionally high efficiency. However, nasal replication occurred, and infectious virus was detectable in nasal swab samples for up to 6 dpi, but sequencing did not indicate accumulation of mutation to that timepoint. Nevertheless, viral adaptation after infection or shedding to naive contact animals or humans cannot be excluded. A follow-up study should include direct-contact animals to assess the biologic relevance of low-level shedding and to clarify the potential role of alpacas in H5N1 transmission. In addition, future studies should include experimental intramammary inoculation of female alpacas to evaluate susceptibility via that route. In conclusion, H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus will likely continue to drive substantial mortality rates in wild birds and marine mammals across North and South America. Risk for virus spillover into domestic animals, including poultry and potentially camelids, will continue considering their large populations on the continents. The demonstrated capacity of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus to acquire mammalian-adaptive mutations heightens concern about cross-species transmission and possible establishment in new mammalian hosts, which could intensify wildlife losses, disrupt livestock production, and generate new zoonotic risks. Sustained surveillance, strengthened biosecurity, and rapid response measures will be essential to limit those impacts. (Continue . . . ) WHO: Bangladesh Reports 4th H5N1 Human Infection for 2026 #19,337 In their latest Influenza at the human-animal interface Summary and risk assessment (8 August to 6 September 2026) - published this week - the WHO has announced the 4th H5N1 case in a Bangladeshi child in the past 9 months. Last April, we saw a fatal case reported from the Chattogram Division, in a child who fell ill on January 22nd, was hospitalized on January 28th, and who died on February 1st. The H5N1 infection was only determined posthumously, via lab analysis on Feb 7th. In early June we learned of a 2nd case, a child from Sylhet Division who was hospitalized on March 28th with a clinical diagnosis of measles with bronchopneumonia. The child was discharged on March 31st, but delayed testing by the IEDCR only revealed a positive H5N1 result on April 20th. And last July the WHO reported a 3rd child - also from Sylhet Division - diagnosed with H5 (later confirmed as H5N1). The child (now recovered) fell ill in May, and reportedly had no travel history and no history of exposure to poultry. In addition to the new H5N1 case in Bangladesh, the WHO also details 3 H9N2 cases in China (previously reported in this blog) and 2 H1N2v Cases from Michigan (reported by CDC here). Avian influenza viruses in humans A(H5N1), Bangladesh On 30 August, Bangladesh, through the national IHR focal point, notified WHO of one laboratory-confirmed human infection with an A(H5) virus in a child from Rangpur division. On 15 August 2026, the child developed a fever, cough and rhinitis and was admitted to hospital on 17 August. On 18 August, a nasopharyngeal swab and throat swab was collected as part of hospital-based influenza surveillance and tested positive for influenza A(H5) by real-time RT-PCR at the icddr,b laboratory on the same day. The sample was subsequently confirmed positive for influenza A(H5N1) at the Molecular and Genomic Laboratory Department of Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR) and National Influenza Centre (NIC) of Bangladesh. Genetic sequencing is underway. The child remained hospitalized and was improving clinically at the time of reporting. There was no reported history of travel outside the area of residence. The child had a history of exposure to duck and chickens, including some that were sick, in the household and adjacent households. Poultry meat and oropharyngeal swab specimens collected from several backyard chickens on 26 August tested negative for influenza A(H5). Close contacts were identified and placed under monitoring and all contacts remained asymptomatic during the observation period, except for two health care workers. Respiratory specimens collected from these two individuals tested negative for influenza A viruses. This is the 4th laboratory-confirmed human case of avian influenza A(H5) reported in Bangladesh in 2026. While full genetic sequencing has not been released, the H5N1 virus circulating in India and Bangladesh is typically clade 2.3.2.1a - not 2.3.4.4b which is currently dominant in much of Europe, Asia, and North/South America. This is the 16th case reported by Bangladesh since 2008 (2 fatal: 1 in 2013 and 1 in 2026), and it reminds us that older clades of the H5 virus continue to circulate, and occasionally spill over into humans. While this is just the 10th human H5 case reported to WHO in 2026 (see chart below), the expectation is that many cases go unreported around the globe. Wednesday, September 16, 2026 #Natlprep 2026: Pandemic Planning At Both Ends of the Spectrum Note: This is the 16th day of National Preparedness Month. Follow this year’s campaign on Twitter by searching for the #NatlPrep #BeReady or #PrepMonth hashtags. This month, as part of NPM26, I’ll be rerunning some updated preparedness essays, along with some new ones. #19,336 Next week (Sept 25th) the U.N. will host a meeting for world leaders in New York City for the purposes of pandemic planning, which will be broadcast live on UN Web TV. As this is a 1 day meeting, and it comes amid headwinds from several directions, it isn't clear exactly what will come from it. Earlier this month, The Lancet published a comment (excerpts below) on this upcoming meeting, which discussed some of the many challenges it faces. From commitment to governance: what should the 2026 UN high-level meeting on pandemic preparedness deliver? Nelson Aghogho Evaborhenea,b Send email to nelsone@ruc.dk ∙ Maureen Lubac,d ∙ Hawi Getnet Degue ∙ Marc Bosonkief ∙ Douglas Muthinji Wanjag ∙ Pimchanok Ratanapisesh ∙ et al. Article Info Published September 4, 2026 DOI: 10.1016/j.langlo.2026.104070 External Link Also available on ScienceDirect External Link Copyright: © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Ltd. Download PDF In September, 2026, world leaders will convene in New York for the second UN high-level meeting on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response (PPPR).1 The first high-level meeting produced a political declaration that reaffirmed commitments to strengthen pandemic preparedness and advance equity, catalysed the WHO Pandemic Agreement negotiations, and emphasised a whole-of-government and society approach to PPPR.1 Since then, member states have amended the International Health Regulations, adopted the Pandemic Agreement, expanded preparedness financing mechanisms, and proposed reforms to the broader global health architecture. These developments represent substantial progress. However, the environment in which they must now operate has changed profoundly. Geopolitical competition has intensified, multiple crises have diverted political attention and financial resources, official development assistance and multilateralism have come under increasing pressure, and the withdrawal of the USA from WHO has accelerated a turn towards nationalism and bilateral approaches to pandemic preparedness,2 adding another layer to an already complex architecture. Meanwhile, regional institutions have assumed greater responsibilities for PPPR.3 In Africa, for example, the revised statute of Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted in 2022 expanded the Africa CDC’s mandate and gave it authority to declare a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security, a power Africa CDC exercised during the 2024 mpox outbreak and again during the ongoing Ebola outbreak, alongside WHO’s declaration of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. Without meaningful coordination, parallel initiatives risk creating overlapping mandates, fragmented financing, and competing expectations relating to surveillance, pathogen sharing, data governance, and equitable access to medical countermeasures.4 Against this backdrop, the credibility of the high-level meeting should not be measured on the basis of yet another ambitious political declaration, but instead, on the basis of whether the meeting delivers a credible governance framework that aligns ongoing reforms, strengthens their coherence, and translates political commitments into sustained preparedness. We outline three priorities. (Continue . . . ) The expectation is that these world leaders will adopt a non-binding "political declaration" on preventing and preparing for future pandemics which was drafted over the summer. While long on good intentions, this document lacks much in the way of `teeth' (enforcement mechanisms, dedicated funding, or even a detailed roadmap). Meanwhile, public health entities and researchers around the world continue to sound the alarm. A few (of many) examples: In April of 2025 the ECDC published ECDC Guidance: Recommendations for Preparedness Planning for Public Health Threats In July 2025 Switzerland Unveiled a New Pandemic Plan Also in 2025, Canada announced plans to Purchase 500,000 doses Of H5N1 Vaccine and the EU announced plans to purchase up to 27 million doses. Last December the ECDC published Pre-pandemic Guidance: Strategies to Fight Avian and Swine flu in Humans And just last month we looked at Referral: Two Related Papers (PNAS & The Lancet) on Preparing for The Next Pandemic Whether these plans - or the vaccines and antivirals being stockpiled - will be adequate or appropriate for the next global health crisis remains to be seen. As we've seen before, No Pandemic Plan Survives Contact With A Novel Virus. But having a framework for dealing with a crisis, and running realistic exercises, can be invaluable when the next pandemic strikes. Most of these pandemic plans are created by - and for - national governments. What planning may be going on at state/province/or local levels - or for the private sector - is harder to discern. But as many people learned to their cost during the last pandemic, it is just as important to be prepared on the individual, family, and neighborhood level. Sadly, over the past few years much of the public guidance that was once heavily promoted by the CDC and HHS on pandemic preparedness has been expunged from their websites. It's as if the first rule of pandemic preparedness in the 2020's is . . . we don't talk about pandemic preparedness. Buried in the CDC's archives, however, are a number of useful documents, including these from 2017 (download them while they are still available): Get Your Household Ready For Pandemic Flu {PDF - 16 pages] Get Ready for Pandemic Flu: Educational Settings [PDF – 16 pages] Get Ready for Pandemic Flu: Workplace Settings [PDF – 16 pages] In addition to the advice offered in these (and other) guidance documents, I'd like to offer 5 things you can do today to prepare for a possibility of seeing another pandemic sometime in the reasonably near future. 1. Get, and become, a `Flu Buddy' The first item is one we've discussed often (see Yes, We Have No Pandemic . . . But Line Up A Flu Buddy Anyway). I first fleshed out the idea in a 2008 blog called Lifelines In A Pandemic. A `Flu Buddy’ is simply someone you can call if you get sick, who will then check on you every day (by phone, social media, or in person), make sure you have the food and medicines you need (including fetching prescriptions if appropriate), help care for you if needed, and who can call for medical help if your condition deteriorates. Those people who care for others, like single parents, also need to consider who will take care of their dependents if they are sick. 2. Avail yourselves of the vaccines that are available now. While the evidence is limited, there are some studies suggesting that getting the seasonal flu vaccine may give you some small degree of protection against the H5N1 virus. Even if it doesn't, it may reduce your chances of having a dual infection, which could either be more serious, or even lead to a reassortant virus. COVID remains a threat, and a dual COVID-flu infection can be worse than either one alone, so if you can get one - keeping current with that vaccine makes sense as well. Since bacterial co-infections are common with influenza, getting the latest appropriate pneumonia vaccines can also a smart move. In 2023, I also updated my Tetanus shot (Tdap), and those over 75 will want to consider the RSV vaccine. 3. Get a Dr. Checkup, Renew Rx Meds, & Handle any Medical Issues Over the past 3 years I've endured two 21-day scalp and face field treatment (Fluorouracil) following my skin cancer surgery in 2024 (and again in 2026). I also got my Rx meds renewed, and have laid in a stock of any OTC meds I might need. 4. Stock up on PPEs or other supplies you might need I went into COVID with an existing supply of N95 masks and gloves, and I refreshed my stocks in 2022, but if you don't already have all the N95/KN95 or other personal protective gear you would want or need during a pandemic, now is the time buy them. Once a crisis begins, it is often too late to stock up. And that goes for any preparedness supplies or gear you might desire in an emergency (Hand Sanitizers/OTC meds/etc.) 5. Be prepared to Shelter in Place If there was one lesson from the opening months of COVID, it is that many of us may elect - or be forced - to stay home, and avoid public places. content: Menu LISTEN LIVE NEWS WEATHER ON AIR PODCASTS BLOGS AGRICULTURE OBITUARIES EVENTS PHOTOS × Sign In Search NEWS WEATHER ON AIR PODCASTS BLOGS AGRICULTURE OBITUARIES EVENTS PHOTOS Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Confirmed in Barron County By Joanna Guza Sep 16, 2026 | 7:46 AM MADISON — The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) has identified a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County. DATCP and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) animal health officials are working together in a joint incident response. The affected premises has been quarantined to restrict movement of poultry and poultry products. Birds on the property were depopulated to prevent the spread of the disease. Birds from the flock will not enter the food system. The HPAI virus has continued to circulate in both wild and domestic birds in North America since December 2021. HPAI viruses are highly contagious and often fatal to domestic poultry. Caused by influenza type A viruses, the disease varies in severity depending on the strain and species affected. The disease can be spread by contact with infected birds, commingling with wild birds or their droppings, equipment, or clothing worn by anyone working with the animals. DATCP continues to urge all livestock owners to implement strong biosecurity measures to protect their flocks and herds from the disease. This includes washing hands, disinfecting equipment, restricting access to animals, and separating new additions to the flock or herd for at least 30 days. Poultry owners are asked, when possible, to keep their birds indoors. When HPAI is diagnosed in a Wisconsin poultry flock, a control area is established within a 10-kilometer area around the infected premises, restricting movement on or off any premises with poultry. To help producers determine if their poultry are located within an active control area or surveillance zone, poultry owners are encouraged to use DATCP’s mapping tool. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) and Barron County Public Health are monitoring exposed farm workers for HPAI symptoms. The risk to the general public in Wisconsin remains low. Find information related to prevention information for farmworkers or others who have close contact with birds, dairy cows, or other relevant animals. DATCP reminds Wisconsin livestock owners to register their premises. State law requires that all livestock owners register where their animals are kept. Poultry is included in the definition of livestock for premises registration. Registration helps animal health officials communicate with flock and herd owners during disease outbreaks. To report increased mortality or signs of illness among domestic birds, dairy cattle, or other animals, contact DATCP by following the instructions on the Animal Disease Reporting webpage. For updates on how the virus is affecting domestic birds in Wisconsin, and to find resources on protecting Wisconsin poultry, visit DATCP’s HPAI in Poultry webpage: https://datcp.wi.gov/Pages/Programs_Services/HPAIWisconsin.aspx. HPAI in Other Species The HPAI virus has continued to circulate in both wild and domestic birds in North America since December 2021. Since that time, the HPAI virus has also affected other species, including mammalian species. DATCP continues to work with USDA to conduct testing for HPAI, encourage biosecurity, and provide resources to producers. For updates on how the HPAI virus is affecting dairy cattle across the country, and to find resources on protecting Wisconsin dairy cattle, visit DATCP’s HPAI in Dairy Cattle webpage: https://datcp.wi.gov/Pages/Programs_Services/AvianInfluenzaCattle.aspx. content_title: FFAR funding takes a closer look at avian influenza transmission
content: INDIANAPOLIS, IND. — The Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research (FFAR) and Entomol Product LLC recently announced $448,940 in grants to test a new approach to reduce avian influenza transmission, commonly known as bird flu. Research will look at whether intermittently fogging or misting hydrogenated catmint oil (HCO) a product with demonstrated antiviral properties, in poultry housing can interrupt transmission of avian influenza viruses. Throughout the poultry and egg industries, avian influenza causes severe economic consequences. When the virus spreads quickly among birds, growers must decide whether or not to depopulate infected flocks. “Producers need practical solutions to reduce avian influenza transmission that work with existing infrastructure to protect their flocks and limit losses,” said Jasmine Bruno, PhD, FFAR scientific program director. “As fogging is a widely used practice in poultry houses, we want to know if it’s a promising mechanism for protecting birds.” FFAR added highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) viruses result in severe disease and high mortality in infected poultry, while low pathogenic avian influenza is a mild or asymptomatic viral infection. HCO is a modified plant essential oil and an EPA-registered active ingredient used in commercially available insect repellents. According to the update, previous research found aerosolized formulations containing HCO significantly reduced H1N1 influenza virus in the air. Research for the project will be led by David Hallahan, PhD, chief science officer at Entomol and Ekramy Sayedahmed, PhD, assistant professor of poultry medicine at Purdue University. The grant will look at using low pathogenic avian influenza to evaluate HCO’s antiviral effects against avian influenza and inform its potential application against highly pathogenic avian influenza. The team is also establishing effective aerosol delivery parameters, including HCO concentration, fogging duration and frequency, effective range and overall efficacy. “Entomol’s hydrogenated catmint oil technology has demonstrated the ability to disrupt influenza viruses in the air and on surfaces at very low concentrations,” Hallahan said. “This FFAR-supported project will allow us to rigorously evaluate its potential as a practical biosecurity tool for poultry producers.” The Rapid Outcomes from Agricultural Research (ROAR) from FFAR is designed to fund research and outreach in response to emerging or unanticipated threats to the US food supply or agricultural systems. FFAR also noted the investments for research to support the US Department of Agriculture’s priorities on Increasing Profitability of Farmers and Ranchers

Conditions Seven Bird Flu Detections Since September 1 Hit Turkey Farms Across the Dakotas, Minnesota and Idaho Published Sep 14, 2026 8:40 AM EDT By Dorothy Brooks YOAV LEMMER | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket Federal animal health officials have recorded seven H5N1 avian influenza detections in commercial poultry operations since the start of September, concentrated in turkey country across North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota and Idaho, according to USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service data compiled in a CIDRAP roundup of the latest detections. The largest was a commercial turkey operation in McPherson County, South Dakota, affecting 61,300 birds. A facility in Turner County, South Dakota, accounted for 43,800 turkeys; a LaMoure County, North Dakota, operation for 41,600 commercial birds; and a Wright County, Minnesota, turkey facility for 29,800. A commercial poultry breeding operation in Edmunds County, South Dakota, housed 30,200 birds. Idaho confirmed two backyard outbreaks in Canyon and Gem counties. Across the past 30 days, eight commercial flocks and six backyard flocks were infected, affecting about 360,000 birds in total, according to the USDA's commercial and backyard flock tracker. For the general public, the health risk remains low. These are animal detections, and no human case has been linked to this cluster. Culling Rules, Not Illness, Drive the Bird Numbers The bird loss figures that appear in coverage of avian influenza can be misleading if read as a death toll from the disease itself. When H5N1 is confirmed in a commercial flock, federal policy requires depopulation of the entire flock, whether or not individual birds are sick. That is what produces totals in the tens of thousands from a single detection. Depopulation exists to stop onward spread to neighboring farms and to limit the amount of virus circulating where people work. It is the reason a single confirmed case at a large operation registers as a larger event than several backyard detections combined. Turkeys are disproportionately represented in these counts for structural reasons. Surveillance in Europe has repeatedly found turkeys to be among the most affected poultry species proportionally, and U.S. outbreak analyses have documented recurring overlap between wild waterfowl activity and turkey farm outbreaks in the Upper Midwest during fall migration. The timing fits that pattern. Early September is when geese and ducks begin moving south through the Dakotas and Minnesota, and environmental contamination from wild birds is the most common route into a commercial barn. Dairy Cattle and Human Cases in the Same Window Two additional dairy herds in Idaho were confirmed infected in the same reporting period. Over the past 30 days, Idaho and Texas together reported H5N1 in five dairy herds, and there have been 88 detections in cattle so far this year. Human infections in the United States have stayed rare and occupational. The CDC has recorded 71 human H5N1 cases since 2024 across 13 states, nearly all in dairy and poultry workers with direct animal contact. Three cases had no identified exposure source, and no sustained person-to-person transmission has been found. The CDC's bird flu situation summary assesses the risk to the general public as low. The cattle side of the outbreak is tracked separately from poultry, on the USDA livestock detections page, and the two datasets do not move together. A quiet month in dairy herds says nothing about what is happening in poultry barns, which is one reason the headline figures can seem to contradict each other from week to week. MedicalDaily previously reported that federal bird flu trackers went nearly a month without updates before a batch of detections appeared in late August. What has changed since is the volume and the concentration: seven commercial detections in the first eleven days of September, clustered in turkey production states as the fall season begins. Food Safety Steps That Have Not Changed Nothing about this cluster changes standard kitchen guidance. Cooking poultry and eggs to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit inactivates the virus. Pasteurized dairy is safe. Raw milk should be avoided, a point federal and state officials have repeated throughout the dairy herd outbreak. The people who need to take specific precautions are those with direct animal contact. Poultry and dairy workers, backyard flock owners, and anyone handling sick or dead birds should use the personal protective equipment recommended by federal health agencies, including eye protection, since conjunctivitis has been the most common presentation in U.S. human cases. Anyone who develops fever, respiratory symptoms, or eye irritation within 10 days of contact with birds or cattle should contact a clinician and say explicitly that they had animal exposure, since that detail determines whether testing for avian influenza is ordered at all. Backyard flock owners can reduce risk by keeping feed and water where wild birds cannot reach them, limiting visitors to the coop, and reporting sick or dead birds to their state veterinarian rather than disposing of them independently. On supply, restraint is warranted. Turkey production runs on a long calendar, and birds destined for the holiday season were largely grown months ago. Whether this cluster affects prices depends on how many more detections occur and where, which is not yet knowable. Large depopulations have historically shown up in retail prices only after a lag of weeks, so the effect of a September cluster, if any, would be a late-autumn question rather than an immediate one. What remains unknown is how far the fall wave will extend, whether the migratory pattern produces the same Upper Midwest concentration as in previous years, and whether federal trackers will update on a consistent schedule. APHIS maintains public tables for commercial and backyard flocks and for livestock, and those remain the primary sources to watch. Seven in commercial poultry operations since the start of September, across North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota and Idaho, including backyard flocks in two Idaho counties. Why are so many birds affected per detection? Federal policy requires depopulating an entire flock when H5N1 is confirmed, so one detection at a large operation accounts for tens of thousands of birds. Is the public at risk? The CDC assesses the risk to the general public as low. U.S. human cases have been rare and confined almost entirely to workers with direct animal contact. Is it safe to eat poultry and eggs? Yes, when cooked to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit. Pasteurized dairy is safe; raw milk should be avoided. Why turkeys specifically? Turkeys are proportionally among the most affected poultry species in surveillance data, and turkey-producing regions overlap with fall waterfowl migration routes. What should backyard flock owners do? Keep feed and water away from wild birds, limit coop visitors, and report sick or dead birds to the state veterinarian. When should someone with animal exposure see a doctor? For fever, respiratory symptoms, or eye irritation within 10 days of contact, disclose the animal exposure to the clinician. READ SUMMARY SUBSCRIBE RECEIVE IN PAPER OTHER EDITIONS Back Animal Health & PathologyOthers Avian influenzaH9n2Infectious bronchitis 14 Sep 2026 H9N2 and IBV co-infection in poultry: Challenges and comprehensive prevention strategies Amid the rise in co-infections and the growing genetic diversity of viruses, effective disease prevention cannot rely on vaccines alone. Valerie Nguyen SAVE IN THE LIBRARY PDF FILE Available in other languages: Tiếng Việt Content available at: Tiếng Việt (Vietnamese) On August 21, 2026, in Hanoi, the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine at Vietnam National University of Agriculture, in collaboration with Kemin Biologics and VINODA, organized a technical seminar titled “H9N2 and IBV Co-infection in Poultry: Challenges and Comprehensive Prevention Strategies.” The event focused on the epidemiological characteristics and pathogenic mechanisms of H9N2 avian influenza virus and infectious bronchitis virus (IBV), while discussing disease control solutions under practical poultry production conditions. The seminar was attended by Prof Bui Tran Anh Dao, Dean of the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine; Prof Nguyen Hoai Nam, Vice Dean; Pham Van Hien, Kemin representative for northern and central Vietnam; Wei Shen, poultry vaccine and health expert at Kemin Biologics; Le My Khanh Huyen, Director of VINODA; as well as experts, speakers and students from the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine. H9N2: Rising risks when co-infection occurs with other pathogens In her opening remarks, Prof Dao said the seminar was one of the practical activities organized to mark the 70th anniversary of the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, while also providing an opportunity to strengthen links between scientific research, education and real-world production. She noted that respiratory diseases remain one of the major challenges facing the poultry industry. H9N2 generally causes milder disease than highly pathogenic avian influenza strains. However, when co-infection occurs with IBV or other pathogens, the severity of lesions can increase significantly. Speaking at the seminar, Dr Dang Huu Anh, lecturer at the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Vietnam National University of Agriculture, emphasized that understanding the genetic characteristics, mutation potential and epidemiological interactions of pathogens is critical to developing effective disease-control strategies. Continue after advertising. Avian influenza (AI) is caused by viruses belonging to the Orthomyxoviridae family and is classified into low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) and highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI). Influenza A viruses are classified according to two surface glycoproteins: hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA). In poultry, 16 HA subtypes and nine NA subtypes have been identified. A key difference between LPAI and HPAI lies in the cleavage of the hemagglutinin protein. In LPAI viruses, the cleavage site is generally restricted to the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts. In contrast, HPAI viruses can be cleaved by proteases distributed throughout the body, allowing systemic infection and resulting in more severe disease. According to Wei Shen, clinical disease severity depends on the virus strain, poultry species, age and disease form. The incubation period is typically one to three days. Poultry infected with LPAI may develop respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms, including serous, mucoid or purulent respiratory discharge and airsacculitis. The disease may also affect the digestive and reproductive systems, reducing egg production and causing misshapen eggs, thin shells or loss of shell pigmentation. Mortality associated with LPAI is generally 0-5%, but it can rise sharply when birds are simultaneously infected with other diseases such as Newcastle disease, IB, Mycoplasma synoviae, Mycoplasma gallisepticum or E coli, particularly when housing conditions and biosecurity measures are inadequate. For H9N2, the risk is particularly concerning because the virus can cause prolonged immunosuppression. It may affect immune organs, interfere with T lymphocytes in the thymus and reduce the ability of birds to mount effective immune responses against other pathogens. Studies presented at the seminar indicated that more than 50% of H9N2 infections were recorded during winter, when cold and humid conditions favor viral survival and transmission. The pathogen may circulate in backyard production systems, commercial farms and live poultry markets. Co-infection of H9N2 with Newcastle disease, IBV, E coli or Mycoplasma can make clinical signs and lesions more severe, prolong disease duration and increase mortality, resulting in significant economic losses for poultry producers. Genetic diversity of IBV increases challenges for vaccine control Infectious bronchitis (IB) is caused by viruses of the genus Gammacoronavirus, family Coronaviridae. It is one of the most common and rapidly spreading infectious diseases in poultry, with an incubation period of only around 24-48 hours. The virus is transmitted primarily through the respiratory route and airborne spread, as well as indirectly through contaminated equipment, vehicles and farm personnel. Following infection, IBV damages ciliated epithelial cells in the respiratory tract and can spread to multiple organs, including the kidneys, gastrointestinal tract and reproductive system. Clinically, birds infected with IBV commonly show coughing, sneezing and watery eyes, accompanied by tracheal and airsac secretions. Nephropathogenic strains may cause swollen, pale kidneys and renal tubular damage. In laying hens, IBV can cause ovarian regression and oviduct damage, reduce egg production by 20–70%, and increase the incidence of misshapen eggs, thin shells and abnormal albumen quality. In broilers aged four to six weeks, the disease can cause severe growth depression, with mortality ranging from 10–60% depending on the virus strain, flock condition and co-infections. One major concern is that vaccinated chickens can still develop IBV infection. According to Dr Anh, this is associated with the virus’s high genetic variability, driven mainly by point mutations and genetic recombination. Because the IBV replication enzyme lacks an effective proofreading mechanism, mutations can accumulate in the S1 gene, a highly variable and antigenically important region. This can lead to the emergence of new variants and reduce the cross-protection provided by certain vaccines. In addition, when poultry are simultaneously infected with multiple IBV strains, genetic recombination can generate viruses with new biological characteristics. A survey conducted in Vietnam from 2014 to 2023 showed considerable IBV diversity, with both GI and GVI genotypes circulating, along with multiple lineages within genotype GI. Wei Shen explained that IBV is currently classified primarily based on S1 gene sequencing, combined with assessments of pathogenicity and in vivo protection. Globally, multiple genotype groups from GI to GVI are circulating. GI-23, particularly the VAR 2 variant, along with certain GVI strains, has been reported in several regions. In Vietnam, different IBV strains have also been detected in both broilers and layers. In some cases, birds have developed simultaneous respiratory and kidney lesions despite vaccination with strains such as Ma5 or 4/91. The continued emergence of new variants is increasing the risk of antigenic mismatch between vaccine strains and field strains. Meanwhile, data on cross-protection between traditional vaccine strains such as Mass and 793B and variants such as QX and VAR 2 remain limited. In addition to IBV, co-infections with ORT, E. coli, Mycoplasma and other pathogens can further increase respiratory pressure. This highlights that controlling a single pathogen is not sufficient to minimize disease risks under modern poultry production conditions. Integrated control from biosecurity to vaccine strategies According to Dr Anh, controlling H9N2 and IBV requires an approach based on the ‘epidemiological triangle’, comprising three key areas of intervention. First, controlling the source of infection. Poultry producers should strengthen surveillance and testing for early detection, while isolating, treating or culling infected flocks in accordance with regulations. Second, breaking the chain of transmission. Comprehensive biosecurity measures should include cleaning and disinfection, control of personnel and vehicle movements, litter management, air quality management, and measures to minimize factors that increase pathogen pressure. Third, protecting susceptible birds. Appropriate vaccination programs should be developed based on the epidemiological situation in the field, combined with measures to improve flock health and resistance. Kemin representatives noted that modern IBV control strategies should begin with biosecurity management, reducing stocking density and improving housing conditions, particularly air quality and litter management. At the same time, active surveillance of potential sources of infection, including wild birds, together with early detection and control of secondary pathogens such as E coli, Mycoplasma and ORT, also plays an important role. Regarding vaccination, Kemin Biologics presented approaches based on global disease surveillance. Kemin’s poultry research center in Egypt monitors migratory bird routes passing through the region, which serves as a crossroads for migration routes from the Middle East, Spain-Morocco and Italy-Tunisia. This surveillance supports the detection, isolation and study of circulating virus strains. Modern vaccine technologies also use oil-based adjuvants such as Montanide ISA 71 VG and Montanide ISA 70 VG to enhance and sustain immune responses. According to information presented at the seminar, the MEFLUVAC-H9ND-16 vaccine demonstrated improved protective efficacy compared with the control product. Under a vaccination program administered at seven days of age, respiratory virus shedding was reported to decline to 10%, while gastrointestinal shedding fell to 20% seven days after challenge. For IBV, given the continuous emergence of new variants, one approach discussed was the ‘Protectotype’ model, which combines different vaccine strains rather than relying on a single strain. Accordingly, when field pressure is primarily driven by variant strains, a variant vaccine such as MEVACTM IB VAR 2 can be used as the initial vaccine, followed by a booster with a classical strain. Conversely, when classical strains are predominant, a classical vaccine can be used as the primer, followed by a booster with a variant strain. Kemin said MEVACTM IB VAR 2 has been evaluated for safety from one day of age and its ability to maintain tracheal ciliary activity. The combination of IB-Var 2 and IB-H120 from the first day of age was also presented as an approach capable of providing cross-protection against the IBV QX strain (GI-19). Experts at the seminar agreed that, given the increasing incidence of co-infections and the genetic diversity of viruses, effective disease prevention cannot rely on vaccination alone. A comprehensive strategy combining disease surveillance, biosecurity, environmental management, control of secondary pathogens and vaccine programs tailored to field pressure will be essential to minimizing losses and maintaining poultry flock productivity. a sea lion for the first time Kyiv • UNN September 13 2026, 08:15 PM • 4982 views A sea lion on Kangaroo Island died from H5N1 after a shark attack. This is the first such case in Australia. Photo: ABC / AA Australia has recorded its first case of a sea lion infected with H5N1 bird flu. According to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), the authorities of South Australia reported that the sea lion, found in the Seal Bay area on Kangaroo Island, was injured in a shark attack and died during its recovery, UNN reports. An examination showed that the animal's cause of death was not a shark bite but bird flu. The authorities said that the injuries may have made the animal more vulnerable to the disease. The authorities noted that the state's sea lion population declines by approximately 2 percent annually, emphasizing that bird flu has a "devastating impact" on sea lion and seal populations in various regions of the world. According to the authorities, bird flu has already been detected in four different mammal species in the state. On June 19, Australia detected its first case of a disease believed to have been caused by the H5N1 bird flu virus, and on August 3, the first mass die-off among wild birds was recorded. On August 25, the country's first case of bird flu among mammals was reported—the disease was detected in a long-nosed fur seal in South Australia. An avian influenza outbreak has been reported in Barron County Wisconsin. Previous outbreaks this year in Wisconsin have been reported in Jefferson, Walworth and Dane counties. BDN file photo Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save MADISON — The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) has identified a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County in northwest Wisconsin. This marks the fifth outbreak among domestic poultry flocks in Wisconsin this year. There have been two outbreaks in Jefferson County, one in Walworth County and this outbreak in Barron County. There also was an outbreak in a backyard flock in Dane County this year. DATCP and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) animal health officials are working together in addressing the Barron County outbreak. The affected premises has been quarantined and birds on the property have been destroyed to prevent the spread of the disease. Birds from the flock will not enter the food system. The HPAI virus has continued to circulate in both wild and domestic birds in North America since December 2021. HPAI viruses are highly contagious and often fatal to domestic poultry. Caused by influenza type A viruses, the disease varies in severity depending on the strain and species affected. The disease can be spread by contact with infected birds, commingling with wild birds or their droppings, equipment, or clothing worn by anyone working with the animals. Cumulative domestic poultry losses since the broader HPAI outbreak in 2022 began in 2022 is estimated to surpass 200 million birds, according to USDA estimates. DATCP continues to urge all livestock owners to implement strong biosecurity measures to protect their flocks and herds from the disease. This includes washing hands, disinfecting equipment, restricting access to animals, and separating new additions to the flock or herd for at least 30 days. Poultry owners are asked, when possible, to keep their birds indoors. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) and Barron County Public Health are monitoring exposed farm workers for HPAI symptoms. The risk to the general public in Wisconsin remains low. Find information related to prevention information for farmworkers or others who have close contact with birds, dairy cows, or other relevant animals. To report increased mortality or signs of illness among domestic birds, dairy cattle, or other animals, contact DATCP by following the instructions on the Animal Disease Reporting webpage. For updates on how the virus is affecting domestic birds in Wisconsin, and to find resources on protecting Wisconsin poultry, visit DATCP’s HPAI in Poultry webpage: https://datcp.wi.gov/Pages/Programs_Services/HPAIWisconsin.aspx. content: (WFRV) - Officials with the Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) have confirmed a positive identification of a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County. DATCP and the US Department of Agriculture animal health officials are working together in a joint incident response. Officials say the affected premises has been quarantined to restrict movement of poultry and poultry products. Wisconsin State Patrol to conduct aerial enforcement in several counties Birds on the property were depopulated to prevent the spread of the disease, and officials ensure that birds from the flock will not enter the food system. The HPAI virus has been circulating in wild and domestic birds in North American since December 2021. The viruses are highly contagious and often fatal to domestic poultry. They're caused by influenza type A viruses and range in severity depending on strain and the affected species. They're spread by contact with infected birds, commingling with wild birds or their droppings, equipment, or clothing worn by anyone working with the animals. DATCP officials urge all livestock owners to implement strong biosecurity measures to protect their flocks and herds from disease, including handwashing, disinfecting equipment, restricting access to animals, and separating new additions to the flock/herd for at least 30 days. And when possible, keep their birds indoors. When HPAI is diagnosed, a control area is set up within an approximate 6-mile area around the infected premises, limiting movement. This DATCP mapping tool can be used to help producers determine if their poultry are located within an active control area or surveillance zone. Wisconsin DHS and Barron County Public Health officials are monitoring exposed farm workers for HPAI symptoms. They say the risk to the general public in Wisconsin remains low. To report increased mortality of signs of illness among domestic birds, dairy cattle, or other animals, contact DATCP by following the instructions on the Animal Disease Reporting webpage . For updates on how the virus is affecting domestic birds in Wisconsin, and to find resources on protecting Wisconsin poultry, visit DATCP's HPAI in Poultry webpage . Alveo Technologies Partners with Alliance Global (AGBL) to Expand Access to Avian Influenza Testing Across Africa, Central Asia and a Portion of the Eastern Mediterranean PR Newswire Mon, September 14, 2026 at 6:02 AM MST 3 min read As outbreaks accelerate worldwide, the agreement brings Alveo's rapid, on-farm molecular diagnostic testing to farmers and health officials on three continents ALAMEDA, Calif., Sept. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Alveo Technologies, Inc., a global leader in rapid, point-of-need molecular diagnostics for early disease detection, today announced a distribution agreement with Alliance Global (AGBL) to bring the Alveo Sense Poultry avian influenza test to farmers, integrators and public health officials across the Africa, Central Asia and a portion of the Eastern Mediterranean at a time when the threat of bird flu has never been more urgent. Alveo Technologies, Inc. Logo Avian influenza is spreading at alarming rates, infecting more than 208 million domestic birds in the U.S. alone and at least 633 million globally, putting farms, supply chains and workers at serious risk. For the agricultural and public health communities in these regions, rapid on-site testing is a critical line of defense to safeguard businesses, protect flocks and reduce the risk of transmission to workers. Under the agreement AGBL has rights to distribute the platform across: Africa Central Asia Select countries in the Eastern Mediterranean region The collaboration combines Alveo's palm-sized diagnostic technology with AGBL's regional network and operational expertise. Together, the companies are addressing vulnerabilities in the food supply chain and delivering rapid, accurate and scalable testing solutions to support compliance, quality control and public health protection. "AGBL's reach across Africa, Central Asia and the Eastern Mediterranean Region gives us a direct path to farmers, integrators and health officials who need reliable avian influenza testing where outbreaks are affecting poultry producers," said Scott Thomas, chief commercial officer at Alveo. "This agreement extends the availability of Alveo Sense Poultry to communities that depend on healthy flocks for their livelihoods and food security." "Farmers, public health and other officials in these regions need a way to rapidly and accurately determine whether flocks are infected with avian influenza so they can take fast action to protect other animals," said Nassim Marie Hambouz, vice president, operations at AGBL. "We're looking forward to providing people in these regions with access to Alveo's revolutionary diagnostic." With this expansive, new AGBL agreement, the Alveo Sense Poultry platform is now available globally, reflecting the company's continued momentum in building a regional commercial network for point of need avian influenza testing. For more information, visit www.alveotechnologies.com. Story Continues About Alveo Technologies Alveo Technologies is a molecular diagnostics company that has developed a portable cloud-connected platform that brings laboratory-quality pathogen detection directly to the Point of NeedTM for farmers, veterinarians and public health officials. By decentralizing molecular diagnostics, Alveo enables rapid detection and decision-making to help protect animal and human health, food security and supply chain resiliency. Its growing portfolio includes molecular tests for avian influenza and other high-consequence pathogens. To learn more, visit alveotechnologies.com or follow us on LinkedIn. About Alliance Global (AGBL) Alliance Global (AGBL) is the largest biomedical distribution group across the Middle East Africa and Asia region with offices in more than 17 countries. AGBL brings innovative technologies and products to researchers clinicians and diagnostic centers in emerging healthcare markets offering distribution consulting and product development services to manufacturers of biomedical technologies. To learn more, visit agbl.net. Featured Highly pathogenic avian influenza confirmed in Barron County Sep 16, 2026 Sep 16, 2026 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save MADISON — The state Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection has identified a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County. DATCP and the U.S. Department of Agriculture animal health officials are working together in a joint incident response, state a press release issued Sept. 15. The affected premises has been quarantined to restrict movement of poultry and poultry products. Birds on the property were depopulated to prevent the spread of the disease. Birds from the flock will not enter the food system. The virus has continued to circulate in both wild and domestic birds in North America since December 2021. HPAI viruses are highly contagious and often fatal to domestic poultry. Caused by influenza type A viruses, the disease varies in severity depending on the strain and species affected. The disease can be spread by contact with infected birds, commingling with wild birds or their droppings, equipment, or clothing worn by anyone working with the animals. DATCP continues to urge all livestock owners to implement strong biosecurity measures to protect their flocks and herds from the disease. This includes washing hands, disinfecting equipment, restricting access to animals, and separating new additions to the flock or herd for at least 30 days. Poultry owners are asked, when possible, to keep their birds indoors. When HPAI is diagnosed in a Wisconsin poultry flock, a control area is established within a 10-kilometer area around the infected premises, restricting movement on or off any premises with poultry. To help producers determine if their poultry are located within an active control area or surveillance zone, poultry owners are encouraged to use DATCP's mapping tool. The state Department of Health Services and Barron County Public Health are monitoring exposed farm workers for HPAI symptoms. The risk to the general public in Wisconsin remains low. Find information related to prevention information for farmworkers or others who have close contact with birds, dairy cows, or other relevant animals. DATCP reminds Wisconsin livestock owners to register their premises. State law requires that all livestock owners register where their animals are kept. Poultry is included in the definition of livestock for premises registration. Registration helps animal health officials communicate with flock and herd owners during disease outbreaks. content: Ad NewsNational News Save Share NewsNational News SubscribeLog In News Home SubscribeLog In Good evening, Your Content Newsletters My saved List Account My Account Logout SectionsMy Region Home Page News Local newsPublic ServiceFederal politicsACT politicsCourt and CrimeProperty and DevelopmentBusiness and FinanceEducationHealthWeather and EnvironmentNational NewsWorld NewsObituariesAustralian of the Year Comment OpinionLetters to the EditorEditorialCartoons Sport LiveToyota HubAFLLocal SportACT BrumbiesCanberra RaidersNRLA-LeagueAustralian RulesCricketNational SportWorld Sport Life and Culture LifestyleFood & DrinkArts & EntertainmentTV GuideThird Party Content Explore Travel DestinationsExperiencesBest OfNewsTips and AdviceRead Magazine Motoring Noticeboard Our PeopleWhat's OnLocal PartnersNewslettersContributePhotos Video Puzzles CrosswordSudokuUltimate TriviaCryptic CrosswordWord SearchCode Cracker Jobs Classifieds AgTraderCountry CarsHorse Deals Tributes & Funerals Sponsored Local FeaturesSpecial PublicationsPartner ContentSponsorships Obituaries Quick Links Today’s Paper Download our app Interactive Puzzles ViewJobs Network View Jobs AgTrader Beevo Press Releases from AAPContact usHelp CentreTerms & Conditions - DigitalTerms & Conditions - NewspaperPrivacy PolicyAbout usConditions of Use Braidwood TimesCrookwell GazetteGoulburn PostThe Queanbeyan AgeYass Tribune Home/News/National News Bird flu strain was always expected to reach Australia By Duncan Murray and Farid Farid Updated June 25 2026 - 10:26pm, first published 8:32am By Duncan Murray and Farid Farid Updated June 25 2026 - 10:26pm, first published 8:32am Save Share Native birds and other animals could be at risk from a major outbreak of a deadly flu strain. Photo: PR IMAGE PHOTO Cases of a new strain of bird flu were always expected to reach Australia's shores at some point, with the disease now detected across two states. A South Australian wildlife rescue centre where a migratory bird tested positive for H5N1 bird flu remained in lockdown as of Thursday. It comes after the nation's first two confirmed cases were reported near Esperance in Western Australia. Wildlife experts believe it is only a matter of time before further bird flu outbreaks. (HANDOUT/Esperance Wildlife Hospital and Sanctuary) Advertisement Ad WA Premier Roger Cook said there was always an expectation the strain would arrive in Australia at some point but the country had an advantage in detecting the initial cases relatively early. "In other countries, it's got into their poultry industry before they even knew it was their area - so the fact that we've got these early lines of sight is really important," he told reporters on Thursday. "We're doing a lot of work with the industry at the moment around what they need to prepare themselves for and how they need to respond." WATCH: Everything you need to know about the H5N1 bird flu strain Volunteers from the Wildlife Welfare Organisation SA collected the first bird to test positive in that state from Knights Beach, roughly 80km south of Adelaide, on June 14. Rescue centre manager Justin Biddle said the team decided to send samples for testing after being alerted to the positive cases in Esperance. "It otherwise looked pretty fit and healthy and it was actually doing quite well in care," he told AAP. "We can't stop migratory birds from entering Australia," rescue centre manager Justin Biddle says. (Dean Lewins/AAP PHOTOS) Advertisement Ad Mr Biddle said there had been no noticeable increase in unwell birds beyond what the organisation generally expected, but more cases appeared inevitable. "We can't stop migratory birds from entering Australia - which is who's going to be carrying it - and it's this time of year where the migratory Antarctic birds start hitting the southern coastline of Australia," he said. Scientists warn the threat of a slew of wild birds becoming infected is "more when than if". "It may not spread in this winter, but it could come from shorebirds ... in the next summer," BirdLife Australia president Hugh Possingham said on Thursday. "It'll probably get here eventually ... that's unavoidable. "The way migratory birds are coming to this continent from other continents and other places - something is going to happen." Three cases of H5N1 bird flu have been detected - two in WA and one in SA. (Susie Dodds/AAP PHOTOS) Advertisement Ad There was currently no threat to humans, federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins confirmed. "Chicken meat and eggs, as prepared normally, are perfectly safe to eat," she said. WA authorities have received almost 200 reports of sick birds since the first suspected case. Authorities confirmed on Wednesday another case of the strain had been detected in a southern giant petrel at Quindalup on the South West coast, north of Margaret River. The preliminary positive result has yet to be officially confirmed and a sample has been sent for further testing. Ground-based surveillance and drone surveys are being conducted at sea lion breeding sites along the South Australian coast, with testing frequency increased in high-risk areas. A temporary ban on all poultry products imported from Australia, imposed by Papua New Guinea's National Agriculture and Quarantine Inspection Authority on Monday, has been lifted. The affected premises have been quarantined to restrict movement. The risk to the general public in Wisconsin remains low. RICE LAKE, Wis. - Avian influenza, also known as bird flu, has been identified in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County. Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) has identified the affected location as Jennie-O in Rice Lake, Wisconsin. Bird flu in Barron County What we know: The affected premises has been quarantined to restrict movement of poultry and poultry products. Birds on the property were depopulated to prevent the spread of the disease. Birds from the flock will not enter the food system. Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) animal health officials are responding. FREE DOWNLOAD: Get breaking news alerts in the FOX LOCAL Mobile app for iOS or Android Quarantine protocols Big picture view: When bird flu is found in a Wisconsin poultry flock, a control area is established within a 10 kilometer area around the area to restrict movement on or off any premises with poultry. To help determine if poultry is in an active control area or surveillance zone, poultry owners are encouraged to use DATCP’s mapping tool. Monitoring illness in humans What we know: The Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) and Barron County Public Health are monitoring exposed farm workers for bird flu symptoms. The risk to the general public in Wisconsin is low. Preventing the spread What you can do: DATCP urges all livestock owners to implement strong biosecurity measures to protect their flocks and herds from the disease. That includes washing hands, disinfecting equipment, restricting access to animals, and separating new additions to the flock or herd for at least 30 days. Poultry owners are asked, when possible, to keep their birds indoors. SIGN UP TODAY: Get daily headlines, breaking news emails from FOX6 News Report signs of illness What you can do: To report increased mortality or signs of illness among domestic birds, dairy cattle or other animals, contact DATCP at 608-224-4872 (business hours) or 800-943-0003 (after hours and weekends). For updates on how the virus is affecting domestic birds in Wisconsin, and to find resources on protecting Wisconsin poultry, visit DATCP’s HPAI in Poultry webpage. content: Skip to main content Download the AppGet your news faster with our mobile experience Install News Weather Sports Chime In Community Watch Live Now 70° Fri 73° Sat 71° Watch Trump holds dinner at the Rose Garden President Donald Trump will host over than 100 hunters, anglers, and outdoor industry leaders for dinner at the Rose Garden. WATCHREAD MORE Montana confirms bird flu in Ravalli County chicken flock by NBC Montana Staff Thu, September 17, 2026 at 1:15 PM Highly pathogenic avian influenza has been confirmed in Ravalli County, marking Montana’s second detection of the virus in 2026. Photo: Associated Press 0Comment Share topics: Avian Influenza Montana Ravalli Poultry Biosecurity Migration CDC HAMILTON, Mont. — Highly pathogenic avian influenza has been confirmed in Ravalli County, marking Montana’s second detection of the virus in 2026. The Montana Department of Livestock confirmed the case on Sept. 17 in a small, commercial flock of chickens. The last affected flock in Montana was found in January 2026. Migratory waterfowl are the primary source of the virus that causes highly pathogenic avian influenza, and the highest risk for disease tends to be during spring and fall migration. Domestic poultry can become infected through direct contact with infected wild birds or through contact with contaminated objects, equipment or the environment. Despite the higher-risk periods in spring and fall, cases in domestic poultry have been observed year-round throughout the country. Other species can also become infected if exposed to large amounts of the virus. Cats and small mesocarnivores such as skunks and raccoons are the most commonly reported. The following was sent out by the Montana Department of Livestock: DOL recommends poultry owners house birds indoors to the extent possible and use good biosecurity practices to minimize disease risk. In addition to practicing biosecurity, poultry owners should observe their flocks at least one to two times a day for any signs of illness. Most often domestic poultry will present with sudden death, but owners may also notice respiratory signs like sneezing, coughing, discolored combs, swollen eyes and lethargy. “HPAI continues to be a risk for domestic poultry in Montana and in many other parts of the country,” said Dr. Emily Kalecyzc, assistant state veterinarian. “While only a small number of Montana flocks have been impacted, the risk to poultry is increased during wild bird migration. Whether you have a large commercial poultry operation or a small backyard flock, ongoing vigilance and increased biosecurity remains important to protect the health of poultry, domestic animals and people.” While HPAI can be spread to humans, the risk to the general population is considered low according to the Centers for Disease Control. However, individuals in contact with potentially infected animals or contaminated objects are considered at higher risk of becoming infected. Public health officials recommend wearing gloves when handling sick or dead birds and washing hands thoroughly after contact with poultry. HPAI is not considered a food safety concern. Existing safeguards keep our food safe and wholesome. These safeguards are why the food supply in the United States is one of the safest in the world. As a reminder, the United States Department of Agriculture recommends cooking poultry to at least 165 degrees Fahrenheit. DOL encourages all poultry producers to immediately report sudden onset of illness or high death loss in domestic poultry to their veterinarian or DOL at 406-444-2976. If you find sick or dead wild birds that have died from unknown causes, please contact your local Fish, Wildlife, and Parks warden, biologist or regional office, or call the FWP wildlife veterinarian at 406-577-7880. content: NZ news Birds Bird flu not cause of death of leopard seal Kate Judson | Wairarapa Times-Age September 15, 2026 • 2:40am MPI chief veterinary officer Dr Mary van Andel says the swabs have been sent to the ministry's Animal Health Laboratory, with results expected within the next two days. RNZ Photo: Supplied Bird flu has been ruled out as the cause of death for a female leopard seal that was found dead in the Hutt River at the weekend, the Ministry for Primary Industries has confirmed. A post-mortem is being carried out on the seal to see if the cause of death can be determined. The Department of Conservation, along with iwi, have removed the seal which had been found dead in the Hutt River. Click here for more details “It is unfortunate, but not uncommon for seals to be found dead for a variety of reasons, including starvation, other diseases and the wider effects of climate change,” MPI chief veterinary officer Dr Mary van Andel said, Read more: High risk of bird flu threat to New Zealand fur seals, experts warn Bird flu could wipe out more than a third of NZ’s endangered native bird species, DOC threat list reveals Looming mass mortality threat on sub-Antarctic Island prompts staff evacuation The female seal was found in the Hutt River on September 13 after being sighted on Petone Beach earlier in the month. A brown skua found on Petone Beach and a kāhu found in Wairarapa both tested positive for the virus in July. A third case of H5 bird flu has been detected in a northern giant petrel, in the Wairarapa. While H5N1 has caused significant outbreaks among wild birds and marine mammals overseas, only those three cases have been confirmed in New Zealand to date. According to a press release from the Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection, DATCP and the U.S. Department of Agriculture animal health officials are working together in a joint incident response. Alveo Technologies Partners with Alliance Global (AGBL) to Expand Access to Avian Influenza Testing Across Africa, Central Asia and a Portion of the Eastern Mediterranean PR Newswire Mon, 14 September 2026 at 6:02 am GMT-7 3 min read As outbreaks accelerate worldwide, the agreement brings Alveo's rapid, on-farm molecular diagnostic testing to farmers and health officials on three continents ALAMEDA, Calif., Sept. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Alveo Technologies, Inc., a global leader in rapid, point-of-need molecular diagnostics for early disease detection, today announced a distribution agreement with Alliance Global (AGBL) to bring the Alveo Sense Poultry avian influenza test to farmers, integrators and public health officials across the Africa, Central Asia and a portion of the Eastern Mediterranean at a time when the threat of bird flu has never been more urgent. Alveo Technologies, Inc. Logo Avian influenza is spreading at alarming rates, infecting more than 208 million domestic birds in the U.S. alone and at least 633 million globally, putting farms, supply chains and workers at serious risk. For the agricultural and public health communities in these regions, rapid on-site testing is a critical line of defense to safeguard businesses, protect flocks and reduce the risk of transmission to workers. Under the agreement AGBL has rights to distribute the platform across: Africa Central Asia Select countries in the Eastern Mediterranean region The collaboration combines Alveo's palm-sized diagnostic technology with AGBL's regional network and operational expertise. Together, the companies are addressing vulnerabilities in the food supply chain and delivering rapid, accurate and scalable testing solutions to support compliance, quality control and public health protection. "AGBL's reach across Africa, Central Asia and the Eastern Mediterranean Region gives us a direct path to farmers, integrators and health officials who need reliable avian influenza testing where outbreaks are affecting poultry producers," said Scott Thomas, chief commercial officer at Alveo. "This agreement extends the availability of Alveo Sense Poultry to communities that depend on healthy flocks for their livelihoods and food security." "Farmers, public health and other officials in these regions need a way to rapidly and accurately determine whether flocks are infected with avian influenza so they can take fast action to protect other animals," said Nassim Marie Hambouz, vice president, operations at AGBL. "We're looking forward to providing people in these regions with access to Alveo's revolutionary diagnostic." With this expansive, new AGBL agreement, the Alveo Sense Poultry platform is now available globally, reflecting the company's continued momentum in building a regional commercial network for point of need avian influenza testing. For more information, visit www.alveotechnologies.com. Story continues About Alveo Technologies Alveo Technologies is a molecular diagnostics company that has developed a portable cloud-connected platform that brings laboratory-quality pathogen detection directly to the Point of NeedTM for farmers, veterinarians and public health officials. By decentralizing molecular diagnostics, Alveo enables rapid detection and decision-making to help protect animal and human health, food security and supply chain resiliency. Its growing portfolio includes molecular tests for avian influenza and other high-consequence pathogens. To learn more, visit alveotechnologies.com or follow us on LinkedIn. About Alliance Global (AGBL) Alliance Global (AGBL) is the largest biomedical distribution group across the Middle East Africa and Asia region with offices in more than 17 countries. AGBL brings innovative technologies and products to researchers clinicians and diagnostic centers in emerging healthcare markets offering distribution consulting and product development services to manufacturers of biomedical technologies. To learn more, visit agbl.net.
